mcqs.q: The access cavity is defined as the opening prepared in a tooth to:
opts: Gain entrance to the root-canal system for cleaning, shaping and obturation
mcqs.explain: The access cavity provides entrance to the canal system so it can be cleaned, shaped and obturated.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the six objectives of the access cavity?
opts: Remove all caries and defective restorations
mcqs.explain: Objectives: remove caries/defective restorations, de-roof, straight-line access, conserve structure, remove coronal pulp, and locate all orifices — not extraction.

mcqs.q: According to Krasner and Rankow, the most important landmark for locating the pulp chamber and canal orifices is the:
mcqs.explain: The CEJ is the most stable landmark and lies at the same level as the canal orifices; its position does not change with decay, crowns, or tilted/rotated teeth.

mcqs.q: Why is complete reliance on the coronal anatomy dangerous when locating canals?
opts: Crowns, decay, tilting and rotation change the coronal picture, but the CEJ stays stable
The crown always hides the pulp
Coronal anatomy is invisible on radiographs
mcqs.explain: Extensive decay, large/unanatomical or destructed crowns and tilted/rotated teeth alter coronal anatomy, whereas the CEJ location does not change.

mcqs.q: The SLOB rule used to differentiate canals on angulated radiographs stands for:
mcqs.explain: With tube-shift, the Lingual object moves the Same direction as the beam and the Buccal object moves Opposite (Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal).

mcqs.q: The 'Law of Centrality' states that the floor of the pulp chamber is always located:
opts: In the centre of the tooth at the level of the CEJ (not applied to molars)
mcqs.explain: The floor lies centrally at the CEJ level; this law is not applied to molars.

mcqs.q: The 'Law of Colour Change' states that the pulp-chamber floor is:
opts: Always darker in colour than the walls
The same colour as the walls
mcqs.explain: The floor is consistently darker than the walls, which helps distinguish it and locate orifices.

mcqs.q: By the 'Law of Orifice Location', canal orifices are found at the:
opts: Junction of the walls and floor, at the terminus of root-fusion lines
Highest point of the pulp horn
mcqs.explain: Orifices lie at the wall–floor junction and at the terminus of the developmental root-fusion lines.

mcqs.q: According to the 'Law of Symmetry', which teeth are the EXCEPTION where orifices are NOT equidistant from a mesiodistal line through the floor?
mcqs.explain: Except for maxillary molars, orifices are equidistant from a mesiodistal line through the centre of the chamber floor.

mcqs.q: With increasing patient age, the access outline of incisors tends to become:
opts: More oval, because the pulp chamber shrinks
mcqs.explain: The chamber shrinks with age, so the access outline becomes more oval; younger patients need a wider access.

mcqs.q: The typical access outline shape for a maxillary central incisor is:
mcqs.explain: Maxillary and mandibular incisors are rounded triangles; canines are oval or slot-shaped.

mcqs.q: A modified 'shamrock' access preparation may be indicated in:
opts: Maxillary molars (extra canal such as MB2)
mcqs.explain: The number, position and curvature of canals may modify the access — e.g. a shamrock outline in maxillary molars to include the extra canal.

mcqs.q: During Step 1 in an anterior tooth, the bur is directed:
opts: Perpendicular to the lingual/palatal surface, ~1 mm into dentine
Parallel to the long axis from the start
mcqs.explain: A small round bur is directed perpendicular to the lingual/palatal surface to penetrate ~1 mm into dentine and draw the outline.

mcqs.q: In Step 2 (penetrating the roof), failing to change the bur angle from perpendicular to parallel with the long axis can cause:
opts: A ledge in the apical third
mcqs.explain: After penetrating the enamel/dentine the bur is rotated to parallel the long axis; not doing so risks perforation of the crown/root.

mcqs.q: The lingual shoulder (lingual triangle) is:
opts: A dentine shelf from the cingulum, ~2 mm coronal to the orifice, removed for straight-line access
mcqs.explain: It is a shelf of dentine extending from the cingulum ~2 mm coronal to the orifice; removing it (and flaring the orifice) improves straight-line access.

mcqs.q: Failure to achieve straight-line access most directly increases the risk of:
mcqs.explain: Without straight-line access the file is deflected and stressed by the axial wall, increasing the risk of instrument separation, ledging, transportation and zipping.

mcqs.q: Which bur is used to remove metal restorations during access, always with water spray?
mcqs.explain: A carbide transmetal bur cuts metal efficiently; water spray controls the heat generated.

mcqs.q: For access through a porcelain or metallo-ceramic crown, the preferred bur is a:
mcqs.explain: Diamond burs are less traumatic to porcelain and more likely to penetrate it without cracking than carbide burs.

mcqs.q: Extended-shank round burs (Mueller/LN burs) are particularly useful to:
opts: Reach the pulp when there is recession/calcification or to remove fibre posts
Cut the external outline in enamel
mcqs.explain: Their long shanks reach a deep or calcified pulp chamber and help remove fibre posts.

mcqs.q: The Endo Z (tapered, safety-tip) bur is used mainly to:
opts: Extend the axial walls and refine margins without damaging the chamber floor
mcqs.explain: Its non-cutting safety tip lets it flare/extend the axial walls and refine margins while protecting the floor and orifices.

mcqs.q: The #17 operative explorer (DG16) is used during access to:
opts: Detect remaining overhanging pulp-roof (ledges) that could cause discoloration/re-infection
mcqs.explain: It detects remaining roof/overhangs; retained roof tissue can lead to tooth discoloration and re-infection.

mcqs.q: Ultrasonic tips in access preparation are especially valuable to:
opts: Refine the axial walls and locate calcified canal orifices
mcqs.explain: Fine abrasive-coated ultrasonic tips allow slow, careful shaving of dentine/calcifications and help find calcified orifices.

mcqs.q: Refinement and smoothing of the access margins (Step 7) is important mainly to:
opts: Prevent coronal leakage that could compromise treatment success
mcqs.explain: Rough/irregular margins promote coronal leakage, which can jeopardise the outcome of the root-canal treatment.

mcqs.q: An oval access outline in a mandibular incisor should alert you to:
mcqs.explain: Some lower incisors have two canals, giving an oval outline; missing the lingual canal is a common error in mandibular anteriors.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is used in Step 5 to confirm straight-line access?
mcqs.explain: A small K-file (size 10) should reach the apical foramen/first curvature with no deflection or pressure from the axial wall. With the endodontic explorer.

mcqs.q: The starting point for the access outline of an anterior tooth is:
opts: The centre of the crown on the lingual/palatal surface
mcqs.explain: Anterior access begins at the centre of the lingual/palatal surface of the crown.

mcqs.q: The 'Law of Concentricity' states that at the level of the CEJ:
opts: The chamber walls are concentric to the external surface at the CEJ
The chamber floor is darker than the walls
The orifices are equidistant from a mesiodistal line
The floor lies in the centre of the tooth
mcqs.explain: Centrality concerns the floor's position; colour change and symmetry are separate laws.

mcqs.q: The Law of Centrality is NOT applied to which teeth?
mcqs.explain: The Law of Symmetry has its own exception — the maxillary molars.

mcqs.q: What are the THREE key factors in access preparation?
opts: Evaluating the external tooth anatomy, visualising the internal anatomy, and locating the CEJ
Outline form, straight-line access and margin refinement
mcqs.explain: These three guide every access cavity before any bur touches the tooth.

mcqs.q: Which objective of the access cavity is concerned with preserving the tooth's long-term strength?
mcqs.explain: The six objectives are: remove all caries and defective restorations, de-roof the chamber, achieve straight-line access, conserve sound tooth structure, remove the coronal pulp, and locate all orifices.

mcqs.q: Round carbide burs (#2, #4, #6) are used during access to:
opts: Excavate caries, create the outline and de-roof the pulp chamber
Extend the axial walls without damaging the floor
Access through porcelain without cracking it
mcqs.explain: Endo Z burs extend the axial walls, transmetal burs cut metal, and round diamonds handle porcelain.

mcqs.q: Fissure carbide burs are used during access to:
opts: Level cusp tips and incisal edges to create working-length reference points
Find calcified orifices by shaving dentine
mcqs.explain: A flat, reproducible reference point is needed before the working length can be measured.

mcqs.q: Which handpiece is preferred for caries excavation during access, and why?
opts: The low-speed handpiece, because it gives more control
The high-speed handpiece, because of its high cutting efficiency
The ultrasonic handpiece, because it does not generate heat
Either — the choice makes no difference
mcqs.explain: High speed is chosen for cutting efficiency when creating the outline; low speed for control.

mcqs.q: A common error in anterior access is failure to find extra canals — particularly a:
opts: Second canal in the maxillary canine
Furcation canal in the maxillary central incisor
Middle mesial canal in a premolar
mcqs.explain: Up to 41% of mandibular incisors have two canals, which is also why an oval outline there should raise suspicion.

mcqs.q: Which bur is used to completely de-roof the pulp chamber?
mcqs.explain: The round carbide #2 excavates caries and creates the outline; the endo access bur completes de-roofing.

mcqs.q: Fissure carbide burs are used in access preparation to:
opts: Level cusp tips and incisal edges as working-length reference points
Remove metal restorations with high cutting efficiency
Reach a calcified canal through a recessed pulp
mcqs.explain: A flat reference point is needed before the working length can be measured.

mcqs.q: Why are round diamond burs preferred for access through porcelain?
opts: They are less traumatic to porcelain and less likely to crack it
They cut metal substructures more efficiently than carbide
They generate less heat and so need no water spray
Their safety tip protects the pulp chamber floor
mcqs.explain: Diamond penetrates porcelain more predictably than carbide.

mcqs.q: A transmetal bur must always be used with water spray because:
opts: Its cutting efficiency causes heat build-up
It blunts rapidly without coolant lubrication
Metal particles would otherwise be inhaled
Porcelain would crack from the vibration
mcqs.explain: Heat control is the stated reason.

mcqs.q: Mueller and LN burs are used when:
opts: There is pulp recession or calcification, or a fibre post to remove
Access must be cut through a metallo-ceramic crown
The lingual shoulder needs to be removed
Cusp tips must be levelled for a reference point
mcqs.explain: Their extended shank reaches deep into a receded or calcified chamber.

mcqs.q: A high-speed handpiece is chosen in access preparation for its:
mcqs.explain: Low speed gives control and is used for caries excavation.

mcqs.q: The access outline form of a maxillary canine is:
mcqs.explain: Incisors are a rounded triangle; canines are oval or slot shaped.

mcqs.q: With increasing age, the access outline of the central and lateral incisors becomes:
opts: Oval, because the pulp chamber decreases in size
Triangular, because the pulp horns become more prominent
Wider, because secondary dentine is not deposited labially
Unchanged, since the outline follows the external crown
mcqs.explain: A smaller chamber yields a narrower, oval outline.

mcqs.q: Some mandibular incisors need an oval rather than triangular outline because they:
opts: Are the smallest teeth in the arch
Have a sharper distal root curvature
mcqs.explain: The second canal widens the required outline labiolingually.

mcqs.q: In step 1, the small round bur penetrates enamel into dentin to a depth of about:
mcqs.explain: About 1 mm, perpendicular to the lingual or palatal surface, before the outline is drawn.

mcqs.q: Enlargement of the canal orifice is also known as:
mcqs.explain: It improves straight-line access and allows effective shaping and cleaning.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is used to determine proper straight-line access?
opts: A size 10 K file or an endodontic explorer
mcqs.explain: The file must reach the apical foramen or first curvature without deflection.

mcqs.q: Which bur is used for removal of the lingual shoulder and enlargement of the orifice?
mcqs.explain: Its safety tip lets the axial walls be extended without gouging the floor.

mcqs.q: Straight-line access reduces all of the following procedural errors EXCEPT:
opts: Coronal leakage at the restorative margin
mcqs.explain: Leakage is addressed by refining and smoothing the margins in step 7.

mcqs.q: Refinement and smoothing of the restorative margins in step 7 matters because:
opts: Rough margins contribute to coronal leakage
Smooth margins make the rubber dam clamp seat better
Rough margins deflect the file from the canal
Smooth walls are needed for the apex locator to read
mcqs.explain: Leakage could risk the success of the whole treatment.

mcqs.q: Which modification of access preparation is used in maxillary molars?
mcqs.explain: The number, position and curvature of the canals can require this modified outline.

saqs.q: List the six objectives of an endodontic access cavity.
saqs.a: Remove caries and defective restorations · de-roof the pulp chamber · achieve straight-line access · conserve sound tooth structure · remove the coronal pulp · locate all canal orifices.

saqs.q: State the three key factors to consider in access preparation and how each is assessed.
saqs.a: External tooth anatomy — crown, root and tooth position; assessed clinically and radiographically. Internal anatomy — chamber and canals; assessed with a straight plus an angulated film and the SLOB rule. The CEJ — the most stable landmark, level with the orifices.

head: Factor
How it is assessed
rows: the crown (remaining structure, coronal seal), the root (number, location, straight or curved) and the tooth overall (straight, rotated, tilted) — assessed clinically (visual, periodontal probing) and radiographically
chamber walls and floor, number and curvature of canals — a straight plus an angulated radiograph, read with the SLOB rule (Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal)
the most stable landmark, at the same level as the orifices — its position does not change with decay, crowns or tooth malposition

saqs.q: State the five laws of access-cavity preparation for locating canal orifices.
saqs.a: Centrality · concentricity · symmetry · colour change · orifice location.

head: Law
Statement
rows: the chamber floor is central at the CEJ level (not applied to molars)
the chamber walls are concentric to the external surface at the CEJ — the tooth-to-wall distance is uniform all round
except in maxillary molars, orifices are equidistant from a mesiodistal line through the centre of the floor
the floor is always darker than the walls
orifices lie at the junction of walls and floor, at the terminus of the root-fusion lines

saqs.q: Name the access burs and the main use of each.
saqs.a: Round carbide (#2,4,6) — caries, outline, de-roofing. Fissure carbide — level cusp tips for reference points. Endo Z — extend axial walls safely. Round diamond — access through porcelain. Transmetal — remove metal. Extended-shank (Mueller/LN) — calcified canals and fibre posts.

head: Bur
Main use
rows: excavate caries, create the outline and de-roof the chamber
level cusp tips / incisal edges to create working-length reference points
extend the axial walls and refine margins without damaging the floor
access through porcelain or metallo-ceramic — penetrates without cracking
reach the pulp with recession or calcification, or remove fibre posts

saqs.q: Describe the seven steps of anterior access-cavity preparation.
saqs.a: Outline · penetrate the roof · de-roof and extend axial walls · remove the lingual shoulder and flare the orifice · confirm straight-line access · inspect with magnification · refine the margins.

steps: Create the external outline — remove caries; start at the centre of the lingual/palatal surface, small round bur perpendicular ~1 mm into dentine
Penetrate the chamber roof — rotate the bur from perpendicular to parallel with the long axis; a 'drop' confirms the pulp (wrong angle risks perforation)
De-roof the chamber and extend the axial walls
Remove the lingual shoulder/triangle and coronally flare the orifice
Confirm straight-line access — a small file reaches the apex or first curvature without deflection
Inspect the cavity with magnification and illumination
Refine and smooth the margins and axial walls to prevent coronal leakage

saqs.q: List the common errors in anterior access-cavity preparation.
saqs.a: Incomplete de-roofing · failure to remove the lingual shoulder · insufficient incisal extension · excessive extension · wrong bur direction or over-penetration · missed canals, especially a lingual canal in mandibular anteriors.

head: Error
Consequence
rows: Incomplete removal of the chamber roof
leaves pulp tissue and compromises visualisation
Failure to remove the lingual shoulder
needless loss of sound tooth structure
especially a lingual canal in mandibular anteriors

saqs.q: Name the burs used in access cavity preparation and state what each is for.
saqs.a: Round carbide burs (#2, #4, #6) excavate caries and create the outline shape and access through the pulp roof. The endo access bur completes de-roofing. Fissure carbide burs level cusp tips and incisal edges to create working-length reference points. A tapered carbide bur with a safety tip (Endo Z) and tapered diamond burs with safety tips extend the axial walls and refine the access margins. Round diamond burs (#2, #4) are used for access through porcelain or metallo-ceramic restorations, being less traumatic to porcelain. The transmetal bur removes metal restorations and must be used with water spray. Extended shank round burs (Mueller, LN) reach the pulp when there is recession or calcification, or to remove fibre posts.

head: Bur
Used for
rows: excavate caries · create the outline shape · access through the pulp roof
level cusp tips and incisal edges — working-length reference points
Endo Z / tapered diamond with safety tip
extend the axial walls · refine access margins
access through porcelain or metallo-ceramic — less traumatic, less cracking
remove metal restorations — always with water spray to control heat
pulp recession or calcification, or removal of fibre posts

saqs.q: State the access outline form for each anterior tooth, and the two factors that shift it towards oval.
saqs.a: Maxillary incisors and mandibular incisors are a rounded triangle; maxillary and mandibular canines are oval or slot shaped; all have one canal. Increasing age decreases the pulp chamber size, giving an oval outline in maxillary and mandibular central and lateral incisors. Some lower incisors have two canals, which also gives an oval outline in mandibular central and lateral incisors.

ans.h: Two things shift the outline to oval
list: Age — the pulp chamber decreases in size

saqs.q: Give the instrument used at each of the seven access preparation steps.
saqs.a: 1 create external outline, high-speed small round bur. 2 penetration of the pulp chamber roof, low-speed round bur. 3 removal of the chamber roof, low-speed round bur. 4 removal of the lingual shoulder and enlargement of the orifice, Endo Z. 5 determination of proper straight-line access, K file size 10 and an endodontic explorer. 6 visual inspection, using magnification and illumination. 7 refinement and smoothing of restorative margins and axial walls, low-speed round bur.

head: Step
Instrument
rows: 2. Penetration of the pulp chamber roof
4. Removal of the lingual shoulder and enlargement of the orifice
6. Visual inspection of the access cavity
7. Refinement and smoothing of margins and axial walls

saqs.a: It allows an endodontic instrument to reach the apical foramen or the first canal curvature without being deflected by the access cavity walls. It provides a direct unobstructed pathway, reduces bending and stress on instruments, decreases the risk of instrument separation, improves tactile sensation and control, allows better instrument contact with the canal walls, facilitates effective cleaning, irrigation and shaping, and reduces procedural errors such as ledge formation, canal transportation and apical zipping.

list: Provides a direct and unobstructed pathway into the canal.
Allows better contact with the canal walls.
Reduces ledge formation, canal transportation and apical zipping.

ans.text: If it was not achieved, re-check steps 3 and 4 and adjust. Failure can result in instrument separation.
